claims.text: Rapidly solidified NiCoCr has minimal local chemical ordering.
Controlled annealing of NiCoCr at approximately 800°C for several hours promotes local chemical order.
Increasing local chemical order makes the local shear-fault-energy landscape more heterogeneous.
The local shear-fault-energy distribution is mediated by local chemical order and associated hard atomic motifs.
A rugged shear-fault-energy landscape increases local barriers to dislocation motion.
Increased local barriers produce greater dislocation pinning and impede dislocation glide.
Greater dislocation pinning promotes serrated flow.
Impeded dislocation glide increases the yield strength of NiCoCr.
Higher-LCO annealed samples will have higher yield strength than rapidly cooled samples when grain size and residual stress are comparable.
Higher-LCO annealed samples will exhibit more pronounced serrations in their stress-strain response than rapidly cooled samples.
Higher-LCO annealed samples will show increased dislocation pinning and jump-like dislocation motion relative to rapidly cooled samples.
Rapidly cooled, low-LCO NiCoCr has a relatively smooth fault-energy landscape.
A relatively smooth fault-energy landscape produces lower yield strength and more homogeneous dislocation motion.
The proposed relationship should hold from room temperature to approximately 600°C when grain size and residual stress are controlled.
Grain-size and residual-stress changes caused by processing could confound the inferred effect of local chemical order.
The comparison should use rapidly cooled and annealed NiCoCr samples with comparable grain sizes and residual-stress states.
The hypothesis is falsified if controlled sample sets show no statistically significant increase in yield strength, serrated flow, or altered dislocation dynamics in the annealed condition.
